newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala's powerful army faces one-third cut.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala's powerful army faces one-third cut.

text.p: A major peace accord finalised by government negotiators and leftist rebels in Mexico on Monday will include a one-third reduction in Guatemala's army, the defence minister said on Monday.

General Julio Balconi confirmed news reports from Mexico City that the two sides had put the finishing touches on an agreement on military curbs early Monday. The partial agreement is due to be signed on Thursday in Mexico.
"In the accord is the reduction of the army up to 33 percent," Balconi told Reuters.

Peace negotiators from both sides of Guatemala's 36-year civil war -- in which more than 100,000 have died -- have met regularly for three months to debate the thorny issue of "Strengthening Civil Society and The Role of the Army in a Democratic Society."
Balconi said the cuts in the 45,000-strong armed forces will affect officers, special forces, and soldiers and will take place within a year of the ending of the war.
The minister also said the accord would give the president power to appoint a civilian to head the ministry of the defence. He added that the army would accept its new role.
"We are the most interested in Guatemala's achieving an enduring peace agreement and if we must we will make a sacrifice and of course we are disposed to do so," he said.
Balconi did not say whether the accord would also limit the army's role to guarding against foreign threats instead of controlling internal security, as it has done for decades.

In the general budget presented to Congress this month the government anticipated reductions in the armed forces, proposing a $15 million cut in army spending for 1997, 11 percent less than the army's $135 million 1996 budget.
The Guatemalan army is the nation's central institution and ran the government between 1954 and 1985.

The army's counterinsurgency tactics and human rights abuses gained international notoriety in the 1970s and 1980s when the army and paramilitary outfits assassinated peasants, labour leaders, students, college professors and other suspected dissidents or guerrilla sympathisers.
The agreement on curbing the army marked the final thematic issue to be discussed as part of a peace agreement that has been negotiated in steps since 1991.

Between now and the end of the year, when both sides say they can reach a full peace accord, the discussions will switch to operational difficulties such as drawing the guerrillas back into civilian life in Guatemala and agreeing on a full ceasefire.
